visuals.heading: Biotechnology Career Path Actually Starts

items.text: The career path in biotechnology is not one ladder, it is three real ladders hiding under one degree.
Common entry titles: Research Assistant, Trainee Scientist, QC Executive, Junior Bioinformatics Analyst.
Every track on this roadmap begins with a degree-stage decision, and that decision decides which rung you land on, not just which subject you studied.
A BSc Biotechnology is the default entry into all three tracks at the lowest rung, Research Assistant, QC Executive, or Junior Bioinformatics Analyst.
A BTech Biotechnology leans toward bioprocess and industrial roles, so it lines up more naturally with the QC-to-regulatory track and process-heavy positions inside the bench track.

blocks.heading: What Actually Changes Every Few Years

items.text: Strip away the specific job titles and the shape of the climb is the same across all three tracks.

Whichever track you land in, bench, QC, or bioinformatics, this stage is about following protocol precisely, documenting everything, and building the one skill that gets you trusted with real work without someone checking every step.
A postgraduate degree changes the shape of this roadmap more than almost any other single decision, and the honest answer depends entirely on which track you are aiming for.
A PhD adds four to six years and is worth it mainly if the actual target is drug-discovery research leadership, a Scientist-grade post at a national lab such as CSIR, DBT, or ICMR, or a faculty role.

blocks.heading: Three Real Progression Tracks, Named and Mapped
rows: Runs existing pipelines (sequence alignment, BLAST searches), writes basic Python/R scripts to clean and organise genomic data.
Builds and modifies pipelines using tools like Nextflow or Snakemake, works directly with wet-lab scientists to interpret NGS results.
Owns the full analysis pipeline for one research programme, makes the call on cloud infrastructure (AWS/GCP) and compute cost, mentors juniors.
Manages 3-6 analysts, owns architecture decisions for tools and pipelines, translates findings for non-technical leadership.
Sets data strategy across multiple research programmes, hires senior technical staff, owns the compute-infrastructure budget.

Any stage where your current employer has no clear next designation above you, regardless of how good your work is.
Bioinformatics, once you have one complete, ownable pipeline you can describe end-to-end, switching before that point means competing on tools instead of outcomes.
